title: The analysis at the real places: tower measures, gauges, open-cell charts and Plancherel bounds
summary: Unit 132 (New/RealPlace) is the analysis at the real places that Theorem B (enough forms) needs. Its first chunk (132-a) sets up the tower method: sizes and gauges (filtrations B_0 ⊂ B_1 ⊂ … of the ring that bound the entries of group elements near a frame), a level (measures θ_l on the floors of the unitary group of a split hermitian space, whose convolution is a Haar measure), pairing kernels averaged floor by floor, and the weight, fibre and Plancherel bounds on each floor; at the complex place it builds the level and the gauge explicitly, proves that the tower measure is a constant multiple of Haar measure with the constant controlled through an open-cell double coset chart (Jacobian and injectivity), and bounds integrals of Bessel functions over that chart. The second chunk (132-b) proves from these tools the local theorem (for a general place, then summed over shells at ℂ), the band limits, and the open-cell, cut-off and volume-kernel bounds.

members.text: Let A be a commutative ring with involution (CommRing A, StarRing A), 𝔰 a shape and T an 𝔰-form over A; V is the free A-module on the basis e_0, …, e_{ϱ−1}, (x_i)_{i∈κ}, z, e*_{ϱ−1}, …, e*_0 with Gram matrix J_T = splitGram(T) and U(J_T) its unitary group. A size for T (Size T) consists of sets B_i = ofSize(i) ⊂ A, i ∈ ℕ, such that: (1) x ∈ B_i and y ∈ B_j imply xy ∈ B_{i+j}; (2) for every finite index type n with |n| ≤ r + 1 (r = 𝔰.r, the number of basis vectors of V) and every f : n → A with all f(a) ∈ B_i, the sum Σ_a f(a) lies in B_{i+1}; (3) for every i and x, −x ∈ B_i ⟺ x ∈ B_i and x* ∈ B_i ⟺ x ∈ B_i; (4) 0 ∈ B_i and 1 ∈ B_i for every i; (5) every entry of J_T and every entry of the inverse matrix J_T⁻¹ lies in B_1.

literature.comparison: Both E and F are complex normed spaces. The variables are redeclared at lines 75–76 without a finite-dimensional assumption. On the ball of radius r the function is complex differentiable and has norm at most B. Restrict to the line through c and z, subtract f(c) and apply a norm-one linear functional on F that norms this difference. The scalar function vanishes at the centre and has modulus at most 2B, so Schwarz's lemma gives (2B/r)‖z−c‖. When B=0 the result is immediate. The statement does not give the derivative estimate or the equality case of Schwarz's lemma.

literature.verdict: Witt extension in matrix coordinates for a nondegenerate Hermitian form with a nontrivial field involution.
literature.comparison: A left inverse for each column map makes its columns a basis of its image. Equality of the two restricted Gram matrices gives an isometry between these subspaces, even when their restriction is degenerate. Every subspace of this finite-dimensional field vector space is a summand. The ambient Hermitian form is invertible. The assumed z with z−z* nonzero gives a trace-one element for the conversion to the quadratic-space statement. For this field and involution the converse coordinate formulation of extension follows by choosing columns for the subspace.

literature.verdict: A one-sided consequence of abelian Plancherel with the compact normalization. Tate's local-field calculation accounts for the local-field case.
literature.comparison: The domain A in General/Measure/Place.lean:18–38 is a locally compact Polish commutative ring with involution, additive Haar measure μ, unitary character ψ, modulus md, units of full measure, and an integrable nonnegative continuous G with G(0)=1 and ∫|∫G(v)ψ(v̄z)dμ(v)|dμ(z)≤c. For η a unit, finite ι and measurable f∈L¹(A^ι), Lean bounds the squared L² integral of its transform by (c/md(η))^|ι| times that of f, allowing infinity. Tate §§2.2.1–2.2.2 use a self-dual measure on a local field. For all such rings the relevant source is Cartan–Godement's abelian inversion and Plancherel. Here is the additional normalization argument. If c is finite, write Θ(z)(v)=ψ(v̄z). Since ∫G>0, continuity of the Fourier transform makes |Ĝ| bounded below on a dual neighbourhood W, so Θ⁻¹(W) has finite measure. For a closed neighbourhood W₀ with W₀W₀⊂W, its inverse image is compact. Indeed, for arbitrarily small open U with positive Haar measure and Θ(U)⊂W₀, only finitely many disjoint translates of U centred in Θ⁻¹(W₀) fit into Θ⁻¹(W). Thus Θ⁻¹(W₀) is closed and totally bounded. This gives closed image and compact kernel. The kernel is an ideal, and units tending to zero preserve that ideal. Their multiplication tends to zero uniformly on the compact ideal, which must therefore vanish. The annihilator of Θ(A) is the conjugate of that kernel, hence zero. Pontryagin duality now identifies A topologically with its full dual. If Θ_*μ=Cμ̂ for dual Haar μ̂, inversion at zero gives C≤C∫|Ĝ|dμ̂≤c. The involution preserves Haar because its positive modulus squares to one. Multiplication by η contributes md(η)⁻¹ in each coordinate. Product Plancherel gives equality at (C/md(η))^|ι|, implying the stated bound. Infinite c, f=0 almost everywhere, infinite right-hand integral and the zero-dimensional product give their immediate limiting cases.

literature.verdict: An explicit rank-one double-coset decomposition with the phase fixed, obtained by unitary transitivity on vectors of equal length.
literature.comparison: The last floor acts on X₀⊕ℂz with X₀ positive definite and z of negative norm. For σ in this floor with last frame entry c satisfying |c|>1, the factors on both sides of cellChart(c) lie in U(X₀) and fix z itself. Knapp's KAK theorem uses a full maximal compact and specifies a radial parameter up to the Weyl group. Here the complex phase of c also labels a double coset, because the stabilizer is smaller. Write the column of the moved z in its X₀ and z components. Preserving the Hermitian norm gives length √(|c|²−1) for its X₀ component. The model boost at ComplexPlace.lean:79–87 has precisely that length and the specified last entry. Theorem 3.4 of Sprehn–Wahl extends the isometry of the two equal-length complex lines to U(X₀). After that left multiplication the columns agree, so the remaining quotient fixes z and lies in U(X₀), giving the right factor. This proves the extra phase and stabilizer assertions in the given range.
sources: A. Knapp, Structure theory of semisimple Lie groups, Theorem 4.10, KAK decomposition <https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~aknapp/pdf-files/1-27.pdf>

literature.verdict: Formal-degree orthogonality accounts for the integral identity. The explicit integrability threshold and normalization require separate work.
literature.comparison: In positive rank the authors transport a particular matrix coefficient through a Hermitian sign frame and multiply it by their formal degree. The conclusion includes continuity, absolute integrability, the inversion law, a nonzero value at the identity and a rank-one identity for every pair of translates. Harish-Chandra's square-integrable orthogonality gives the formal-degree factor after choosing Haar measure. Square integrability alone does not give absolute integrability. I found no place in the cited paper identifying this coefficient and compact-dual Haar measure with the explicit large-gap condition of the pinned code. The Lean proof uses a prior large-gap theorem and proves the frame transport.
sources: Harish-Chandra, Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups II, pp. 87–88, definition and square-integrable orthogonality <https://archive.ymsc.tsinghua.edu.cn/pacm_download/117/6013-11511_2006_Article_BF02392813.pdf>

literature.verdict: The stated upper bound follows from an exact iterated beta integral with translations and a linear change in each row.
literature.comparison: Write k for the number of columns, m for the number of integrated rows and p for the current determinant exponent. Integrating one complex row against positive definite M gives a factor π^k Γ(p−k)/(Γ(p)|det S|²) times det(M)^(1−p). Translate by the prescribed row offset, use the complex change of variables and the determinant lemma, and evaluate the resulting radial integral. The successive integer exponents run from m+r down to r+1. Since r≥k, each gamma quotient is at most 1/k!, giving the displayed power and the factor det(M)^(−r). Empty rows or columns give the direct constant case. The beta identity is located precisely. I did not locate this normalization and translated inequality as a numbered result in Hua's book.

imports.text: Ostrowski–Taussky: H ⪰ 0 and Θ + Θᴴ − H ⪰ 0 imply |det H| ≤ 2^n|det Θ|.

literature.verdict: Equivalent to the determinant inequality for a matrix with positive Hermitian part, including its semidefinite endpoint.
literature.comparison: Set R=(Θ+Θ*)/2. Lean permits any positive semidefinite H≤2R and gives |det H|≤2^n |det Θ|. If H is singular the inequality is immediate. Otherwise R is positive definite, determinant monotonicity gives det H≤2^n det R, and Ostrowski–Taussky gives det R≤|det Θ|. Conversely H=2R recovers the usual inequality for R>0. This equivalence concerns the inequality only. The declaration includes no equality criterion.
sources: Ostrowski and Taussky, On the variation of the determinant of a positive definite matrix, Indagationes Mathematicae 13 (1951), 383–385. The inequality is identified and restated in the introduction on p. 331 of this paper <https://www.kurims.kyoto-u.ac.jp/EMIS/journals/AMEN/2022/AMEN-210209.pdf>
